title: Nobody talks about her long enough to remember her name.
paragraphs: Nobody talks about her long enough to remember her name.
That is the tragedy.

Not because she did not matter…
but because people only remembered what was done to her.

Some women in Scripture are quoted.
Some are honored.
Some are preached about every Mother’s Day.

But some women…
were used by broken men,
judged by religious people,
discarded by society,
and almost erased by history.
One of them walked into a Pharisee’s house carrying an alabaster jar and a shattered reputation.
Another bent over a well under the heat of noon because shame had taught her to avoid eye contact.
Another bled for twelve years while people treated her pain like contamination.
Another was dragged through the streets by men pretending to care about holiness while secretly weaponizing her humiliation.

And one…
one unnamed concubine in Judges 19…
was abused, abandoned, violated, dismembered, and forgotten so brutally that many pastors avoid the passage entirely.
Yet God left her story in Scripture.
Not to entertain us.
To expose us.
Because the Bible does not sanitize human evil.
It reveals it.

And somewhere in these women’s stories…
millions of people quietly recognize themselves.

Used.
Touched but unloved.
Needed but not valued.
Seen as a body before a soul.
Judged for survival decisions.
Silenced after trauma.
Remembered for scandal instead of suffering.
And maybe that is why Jesus kept walking toward women everybody else walked away from.
The Bible says in John 4 that Jesus “must needs go through Samaria.”
The Greek says:

“ἔδει δὲ αὐτὸν διέρχεσθαι διὰ τῆς Σαμαρείας”
(edei de auton dierchesthai dia tes Samareias)
The word “ἔδει” (edei) means “it was necessary,” “it was divinely required.”
He was not lost.
He was sent.
Toward a woman nobody respected.
Toward a woman men talked about but never truly saw.
Toward a woman carrying relational wreckage like chains around her soul.
The Samaritan woman had been married five times.
Most sermons stop there.
But history matters.
Context matters.

Women in first-century Samaria often had very little legal authority in divorce proceedings. A woman repeatedly abandoned or passed between men was not automatically promiscuous. She could have been discarded repeatedly by men who used her, rejected her, or died.
And when Jesus says:

“you have had five husbands”
(John 4:18)
He does not say it with cruelty.

The Greek contains no mockery.
No humiliation.
No disgust.
Only revelation.
Truth without contempt.
That alone heals something in people.
Because most of us have met people who expose our failures to feel powerful.
Jesus exposed wounds to restore people.
And the woman at the well immediately shifts the conversation toward worship because wounded people often hide behind theology when they feel spiritually naked.
But Jesus keeps reaching deeper.
Then comes one of the most astonishing revelations in Scripture.
Jesus openly reveals His Messiahship to this broken Samaritan woman before many others.
“I who speak to you am He.”
In Greek:

“ἐγώ εἰμι”
(egō eimi)
“I AM.”
The same echo connected to the divine revelation in Exodus.
In Hebrew, when God speaks to Moses through the burning bush:

“אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה”
(Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh)

“I AM THAT I AM.”
(Exodus 3:14)
Imagine this moment.

A woman carrying relational shame…
hears the voice of the Eternal God speaking identity directly into her brokenness.
Not after she fixed herself.
Not after religious people approved her.
Not after she cleaned up her past.

At the well.
In the middle of her mess.
And suddenly the woman hiding from society becomes the first evangelist to her city.
That is what Jesus does.
He turns rejected people into revival carriers.
But religion often does the opposite.
In John 8, the woman caught in adultery is dragged publicly before Jesus.
Notice something disturbing.
Where was the man?
The Law of Moses required both participants to be judged.
But hypocrisy always targets the vulnerable first.

The men hold stones.
The woman holds shame.
And the Greek wording matters deeply.

“κατειλημμένην ἐπ’ αὐτοφώρῳ μοιχευομένην”
(kateilēmmenēn ep’ autophōrō moicheuomenēn)
Caught “in the very act.”

Not accused.
Not rumored.
Exposed completely.
Can you imagine her terror?

Hair disheveled.
Body trembling.
Eyes avoiding the crowd.
People staring not with compassion…
but with appetite.
Because public shame attracts spectators.
Then Jesus kneels.
The Creator bends lower than the accused woman.
And while everybody else prepares to throw stones…
God starts writing in the dirt.

The only finger in Scripture that once wrote commandments onto stone tablets…
now writes beside a condemned woman.
People speculate endlessly about what He wrote.
But perhaps the greater miracle is this:
He stayed.
Everyone else used her moment to prove a point.
Jesus used the moment to save a soul.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone.”

One by one…
the stones hit the ground instead of her body.
And then Jesus asks:
“Woman, where are those thine accusers?”

In Greek:
“Γύναι, ποῦ εἰσιν;”
(Gynai, pou eisin?)
“Woman, where are they?”

Not “adulteress.”
Not “failure.”
Not “disgrace.”
Woman.
Dignity restored before behavior corrected.
And then:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Notice the order.

Mercy first.
Transformation second.
Modern religion often reverses it.
That is why so many wounded people run from church while still secretly starving for God.
Then there is the woman with the issue of blood.
Twelve years bleeding.
Twelve years isolated.
In Levitical law, constant bleeding rendered someone ceremonially unclean.
Meaning people avoided her touch.
Imagine what prolonged rejection does to the nervous system.
To self-worth.
To identity.
Mark 5 says she had:
“suffered many things of many physicians.”
The Greek:

“πολλὰ παθοῦσα”
(polla pathousa)
She suffered greatly.

Not only physically.
Financially.
Emotionally.
Socially.
And yet she says within herself:
“If I may touch but his garment, I shall be whole.”
The word for “whole” is:

“σωθήσομαι”
(sōthēsomai)
Not merely healed physically.

Saved.
Restored.
Made complete.
And when she touches Jesus…
He stops.

In a crowd full of people touching Him casually…
Jesus recognizes the touch of desperate faith.
And when she trembles before Him publicly…
He calls her:
“Daughter.”
The only recorded time in the Gospels Jesus directly calls a woman “daughter.”
Do you understand how healing that is?
Some people had not called her anything compassionate for years.
Then there is the sinful woman in Luke 7.
She enters Simon the Pharisee’s house carrying alabaster and tears.
The Greek describes her as:

“γυνὴ…ἥτις ἦν ἐν τῇ πόλει ἁμαρτωλός”
(gynē… hētis ēn en tē polei hamartōlos)
“A woman… who was known in the city as sinful.”
Everybody knew her reputation.

That means when she entered the room…
people probably whispered immediately.
There she is.
People love labeling women permanently by seasons God intended to redeem temporarily.
But she kneels at Jesus’ feet weeping.
Not elegant tears.
Violent grief.
The Greek implies continual weeping.
Her tears become water for His feet because nobody else honored Him properly.
Then she wipes His feet with her hair.
Do you understand the scandal?
In Jewish culture, a woman unbinding her hair publicly could be viewed as deeply shameful.
But broken people stop caring about appearances when they finally encounter real mercy.
Simon silently judges her.
And Jesus answers thoughts Simon never spoke aloud.
That alone should terrify prideful religion.
Then Jesus says:
“Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much.”
Not because her tears purchased salvation.
But because forgiven people love differently.
People who know they were rescued from drowning do not clap politely for Jesus.
They collapse at His feet.
But perhaps the darkest story remains in Judges 19.
The unnamed concubine.
One of the most horrifying accounts in all Scripture.

A Levite uses her.
Abandons her.
Throws her outside to violent men.
And while she is brutalized through the night…
he sleeps.
In the morning he opens the door and says:
“Get up; let us be going.”

No tenderness.
No grief.
No urgency.
Only coldness.
The Hebrew narrative is intentionally horrifying because God wanted future generations to see what happens when people lose the fear of the Lord.
The concubine has no recorded voice.
No recorded prayer.
No recorded defense.
Just suffering.
And millions of wounded people understand exactly what that silence feels like.
Because some trauma steals language.
Some pain becomes unspeakable.

Yet even here…
Scripture refuses to hide the evil done against women.
The Bible does not glorify abuse by recording it.
It condemns the darkness of the human heart.
And if you read carefully through the entire Gospel story…
you notice something revolutionary for the ancient world:
Jesus consistently restored dignity to women.

He spoke publicly with them.
Taught them.
Defended them.
Healed them.
Appeared first to them after resurrection.

In a culture where women’s testimony was often dismissed in court…
God chose women as the first witnesses of the risen Christ.
That was not accidental.
And when Mary Magdalene wept outside the empty tomb…
Jesus spoke her name.

“Μαριάμ”
(Mariam)
One word.
But sometimes hearing your name from God heals years of being objectified by people.
Maybe that is why these stories still shake people today.
Because this world still uses people.

Still markets bodies.
Still profits from insecurity.
Still humiliates failure publicly.
Still throws stones digitally.
Still confuses lust with love.
Still abandons the wounded after consuming them emotionally.
And many people reading this have become experts at smiling while bleeding internally.
Some were touched before they were treasured.
Some learned attention is not the same thing as love.

Some carry secret shame from things done to them…
or things they did trying to survive loneliness.
Some have spent years believing God looks at them the way cruel people did.

But Jesus does not approach broken people the way predators do.
Or the way self-righteous people do.

He tells the truth completely…
without removing dignity.
That combination is rare on earth.
And maybe you have been forgotten by people.

Maybe your story got reduced to one mistake.
One relationship.
One addiction.
One trauma.
One season.
One scandal.
But heaven does not archive people the way society does.
Jesus still walks toward wells at noon.
Still kneels beside condemned people.
Still stops for trembling women hidden in crowds.
Still speaks names with tenderness.
Still restores what shame tried to erase.
Still resurrects identities buried under public opinion.
And maybe the deepest wound is not what happened to you…
but believing it defined you permanently.
It did not.
The cross already saw every secret before you were born.
And Christ still chose nails.
That means your worst chapter met mercy before you even lived it.
Somebody reading this has been surviving off crumbs of validation while starving for real love.
Somebody has spent years punishing themselves for something Jesus already died to forgive.
Somebody has believed God tolerated them instead of desired them.
But the Gospel is not Jesus searching for perfect people.
It is Jesus rescuing ruined people.
That is the entire story.

And maybe tonight…
for the first time in years…
you need to stop identifying yourself by what people called you.

Because if Christ calls you redeemed…
healed…
daughter…
forgiven…
restored…
then shame no longer has legal authority over your identity.
Follow for daily biblical truth, healing, conviction, discipleship, and encouragement rooted fully in Jesus Christ.

Some people were only loved for what they provided…
until Jesus loved them for who they truly were.
